name: Homocystinuria

prevalence.estimate: 1 in 200,000 to 1 in 335,000 (worldwide); 1 in 65,000 in Ireland

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Biochemical and genetic criteria for classical homocystinuria

criteria.description: Markedly elevated plasma total homocysteine (typically >100 micromol/L)
Low or absent plasma cystathionine and cysteine
Positive urinary cyanide-nitroprusside test (detects disulfides including homocystine)
Biallelic pathogenic variants in CBS gene
Reduced CBS enzyme activity in fibroblasts or liver

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Markedly elevated plasma homocysteine and methionine, confirmed by CBS enzyme assay or genetic testing. Must distinguish from other causes of hyperhomocysteinemia.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: About 50% of patients are pyridoxine (vitamin B6) responsive, which is associated with a milder phenotype. Newborn screening can detect elevated methionine but has limited sensitivity for B6-responsive forms.

pathognomonic.notes: Typically downward and nasal; distinguishes from Marfan (upward and temporal). Present by age 10 in most untreated patients.

common.symptomName: Skeletal abnormalities (marfanoid habitus, tall stature, long limbs)

common.notes: Present in >50% by age 16 if untreated
Less common in B6-responsive patients; may range from mild learning difficulties to severe disability
Both arterial and venous; major cause of morbidity and mortality. Risk by age 30 is ~50% if untreated.

rare.notes: Can occur at young ages; both ischemic stroke and cerebral venous sinus thrombosis

laboratory: Markedly elevated plasma total homocysteine (typically >100 micromol/L; often >200 in untreated classical form)
Elevated plasma methionine (distinguishes from remethylation defects where methionine is low)
Low or absent plasma cysteine and cystathionine
Elevated methionine on newborn screening (variable sensitivity)
imaging: Skeletal X-rays showing osteoporosis, vertebral fractures, long bone abnormalities
MRI brain may show white matter changes or evidence of prior stroke
Doppler ultrasound for venous thrombosis detection
DEXA scan for bone density assessment
genetic: Biallelic pathogenic variants in CBS gene (chromosome 21q22.3)
I278T mutation common in B6-responsive patients (Celtic origin)
G307S mutation common in B6-non-responsive patients
other: Slit-lamp examination for ectopia lentis detection
Pyridoxine (B6) responsiveness trial (200-1000 mg/day for 6 weeks)
Thrombophilia workup if thromboembolic event occurs

distinguishingFeatures: Marfan has upward and temporal lens subluxation (homocystinuria is downward/nasal)
Marfan has aortic root dilation; homocystinuria has thromboembolism
B12 deficiency has elevated homocysteine but normal or low methionine
Megaloblastic anemia present in B12 deficiency
Methylmalonic acid elevated in B12 deficiency
MTHFR deficiency has low or normal methionine (not elevated)
Sulfite oxidase deficiency has elevated sulfite and thiosulfate
Ectopia lentis present but different biochemical profile
Low uric acid in molybdenum cofactor deficiency

redFlags: Thromboembolic event in young person (stroke, DVT, PE) - test for homocystinuria
Ectopia lentis with marfanoid habitus - differentiate from Marfan syndrome
Perioperative thrombosis risk (ensure adequate hydration and consider anticoagulation for surgery)
Nitrous oxide anesthesia contraindicated (further impairs homocysteine metabolism)
Untreated newborns deteriorating rapidly - emergency treatment needed
references: Morris AAM, et al. Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2017;40(1):49-74.
Sacharow SJ, Picker JD, Levy HL. Homocystinuria Caused by Cystathionine Beta-Synthase Deficiency. In: Adam MP, et al., eds. GeneReviews. University of Washington, Seattle; 2004 [Updated 2017].
Mudd SH, et al. The natural history of homocystinuria due to cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency. Am J Hum Genet. 1985;37(1):1-31.
Yap S. Classical homocystinuria: vascular risk and its prevention. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2003;26(2-3):259-65.
